blocks.title: How child support is usually figured in New York
body: New York uses a formula set out in the Child Support Standards Act. In general, it starts with both parents' incomes, applies a percentage based on the number of children, and splits the result between the parents based on their share of the combined income.
Courts can also add a share of costs like child care, health insurance, unreimbursed medical costs, and sometimes education.
The court can depart from the formula in some situations. A lawyer can explain how this may apply to you.

blocks.title: Common mistakes on this form
body: Mixing up gross pay (before deductions) and take-home pay (after deductions).
Leaving out cash work, tips, side jobs, or benefits.
Using different time periods without saying so — for example, weekly pay on one line and monthly on another. This app asks "how often" for every amount to help avoid this.
Forgetting to bring the required papers, like recent pay stubs and tax returns.
Signing without reading every line. The form is a sworn statement.

blocks.title: If this is a new child support case
body: Cases are often heard by a Support Magistrate in Family Court. Both parents are usually asked to bring this form and their financial papers.
If you don't have all your papers by the court date, bring what you have and tell the court what is missing.
The court may set a temporary order while the case continues.

blocks.title: If you are asking to change an existing order
body: Under New York law (Family Court Act § 451), a court may change a child support order if there has been a substantial change in circumstances. It may also change it if three years have passed since the order was made or last changed, or if either parent's gross income has changed by 15% or more — unless the parents agreed in writing to opt out of these. A drop in income counts only if it was not voluntary and the parent tried hard to find similar work.
Whether any of these applies to you is a legal question. Bring a copy of the current order and papers showing what has changed since it was made.

A change does not happen automatically. Until the court changes the order, the existing order stays in effect, and support that is already past due generally can't be reduced. That is why many people file as soon as things change.

blocks.title: If this case is about an order not being paid
body: Bring a copy of the order and any payment records, such as a statement from the Support Collection Unit or your own records of payments made or missed.
Unpaid support (arrears) is treated seriously by the court. The court has several ways to enforce orders.
Because the consequences can be significant for both parents, legal advice can be especially helpful in these cases.

blocks.title: If you are concerned the amount is too high
body: Courts look at income from all sources, and this form must be complete and true. Leaving out income can lead to serious consequences.
Courts generally look closely at a voluntary drop in income, such as quitting a job. In some situations a court may count income a parent could earn, not just what they earn now.

What you can do is make sure the court has the full picture: bring papers for every expense you list, proof of other support orders you pay, and proof of health insurance and child care costs you pay.
A lawyer can explain whether anything in your situation could affect the amount.

blocks.title: If you are concerned the amount is too low
body: The court decides support based on information from both parents. If you have papers showing the other parent's income (for example, pay stubs, job information, or business records), bring them.
Costs such as child care, health insurance, and medical expenses may be considered in addition to basic support. Bring receipts and proof of what you pay.
A lawyer can explain how the court may look at the other parent's income and these added costs.

blocks.title: Getting to a fair amount
body: The formula is meant to produce a consistent result from complete information. The most useful thing you can do is make your form accurate and complete, and bring papers that back up each number.
If something about your situation is unusual — for example, a child with special needs, or very high or very low incomes — tell the court and consider legal advice.

blocks.title: Understanding the process
body: Support cases usually move through one or more court dates where each parent's finances are reviewed.

After a Support Magistrate decides, a parent who disagrees can file written objections. The deadline is short and strict: generally 30 days after the order is given to you in court or served on you, or 35 days after it is mailed to you. Ask the court or a lawyer about the deadline in your case as soon as you get a decision.
Free legal help programs and the court's help center can explain each step.

blocks.title: If you and the other parent were never married
body: Parentage (who the legal parents are) usually needs to be established before support is ordered. This can happen through an Acknowledgment of Parentage or a court order.
If parentage hasn't been established yet, the court may handle that first.

blocks.title: Not sure where you stand?
body: That's common. Your court papers usually say what the case is about and who filed it. The court's help center or a legal aid program can help you read them.
